characters: Yiadom: a nine-year-old Ghanaian boy with short-cropped hair in a yellow shirt and khaki-brown school shorts.
Lobnibe: his nine-year-old Ghanaian female classmate with neat cornrows and green hair beads, wearing a yellow shirt and brown school pinafore, holding a small magnifying hand lens.
Their teacher: a friendly Ghanaian female Primary 4 teacher in a warm ochre-and-green African-print dress.

narrationPlan.voice: A thoughtful boy’s voice for Yiadom; a bright girl’s voice for Lobnibe
narrationPlan.pace: Careful and curious, like a close look (about 100 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A soft garden tune with a gentle lift (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Children across Ghana observe weeds and crops in school gardens and family farms. The story follows the NaCCA Basic 4 Science standard on the parts of a plant and their functions (B4.2.2.1.1).
The coloured-water experiment uses safe food colouring under teacher supervision; learners wash hands after handling soil and never taste unknown plants.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check the jobs given for roots, stem, leaves, and flower against NaCCA B4.2.2.1.1.
Check that the story relates each part’s job to its position on the plant.

teacherGuide.overview: Children examine a young plant to learn what its roots, stem, leaves, and flower do, and observe a coloured-water transpiration test that makes stem transport visible. Based on NaCCA Basic 4 Science.
learningGoals: Name the four main parts of a flowering plant.
State the main function of roots, stem, leaves, and flowers.
Explain how each part’s position suits its function.

subjectLinks.subject: Science (NaCCA B4.2.2.1.1)
subjectLinks.link: Parts of a plant and their functions

beforeReading: Ask: why do you think roots grow underground while leaves spread out in the air?
whileReading: Let learners inspect a safe uprooted weed with a hand lens.
afterReading: Draw a flowering plant and explain one job of each part.
Set up the food-colouring and white-flower stem test overnight.
discussion: What would happen to a plant if it lost its roots?
Why do leaves grow where sunlight can reach them?
reflection: Which part of a plant do you think works hardest, and why?

support: Provide a plant diagram and match each part to its function card.
stretch: Investigate how insects like bees help flowers form fruits and seeds.

culturalNotes: Children across Ghana observe weeds and crops in school gardens and family farms. The story follows the NaCCA Basic 4 Science standard on the parts of a plant and their functions (B4.2.2.1.1).
The coloured-water experiment uses safe food colouring under teacher supervision; learners wash hands after handling soil and never taste unknown plants.
localiseThis: Use safe, non-irritating weeds from your school compound and food colouring for the water jar.
Wash hands thoroughly after touching soil and plants; never taste unknown plants.

factCheck.claim: Roots anchor the plant and absorb water, stems support the plant and transport water upward, green leaves make food using sunlight, air, and water, and flowers produce seeds.
factCheck.explanation: Core upper-primary plant structure and function concepts, with coloured-water uptake demonstrating xylem transport through the stem.
